title: The lost princess
hookLine: Rebbe Nachman's tale of a viceroy who searches for years for a lost princess

cards: One careless sentence, said in anger, and a king loses his daughter. That's how the first of Rebbe Nachman's tales begins. He didn't only teach.
In his last years he started telling stories, fairy tales really: kings and princesses, giants, deserts, enchanted palaces. They can sound like bedtime stories.
He treated them as anything but: his student Nathan wrote them down, and Breslov tradition reads them as teachings in disguise.

teach.b: Here's the story, in short strokes. A king has a daughter he loves dearly. One day, angry with her, he blurts out: may the not-good take you.
The next morning, she's gone. The king is heartbroken. His viceroy, his second-in-command, asks for a servant, a horse and some money, and sets out to find her.
He searches for years. At last he finds her, held in a strange palace. She tells him how to free her: choose a place, long for her for a whole year, and on the last day, fast and stay awake.
On the last day, he sees an apple, eats it, and falls into a deep sleep. He fails. She gives him a second chance: this time he may eat, but he must not drink wine.

teach.h: AN APPLE. A SPRING. SEVENTY YEARS.
teach.b: He finds a spring that looks and smells like wine, drinks, and sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, she's been taken farther away.
All that's left is her kerchief, with a message written in her tears: now look for me on a mountain of gold, in a castle of pearl.
So he gets up and keeps searching, through deserts and giants. The tale's last line is strange: how he freed her, the story doesn't tell. But in the end, he freed her.
Breslov teachers read the princess as the Divine Presence in exile, and the viceroy as every person who has lost something holy and is trying to find it again. He isn't a hero because he never fails.
He fails twice, badly. He's a hero because the story always says the same thing next: and he kept searching.

how: Rebbe Nachman's thirteen tales, collected as Sippurei Ma'asiyot, are read and studied by Breslov Hasidim and many others, often with commentaries that explain their hidden meanings.

o: a royal guard who protects the king's family
a king's son, next in line for the throne
a king's deputy who rules or acts in his name

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.

s: the viceroy frees the princess on his first try
he fails twice: once after an apple, once after drinking from a spring.
the tale never tells how he freed her
it only says that in the end, he did.
Breslov teachers read the princess as the Divine Presence in exile
and the viceroy as anyone searching for something holy they've lost.

games.q: you're the viceroy. you've failed twice and slept seventy years. all that's left is her kerchief. what do you do?
o: go home. you had your chances.
keep searching, toward the mountain of gold.
stay where you are and wait for her to return.
games.why: he gets up and keeps searching. the tale ends: how he freed her isn't told, but in the end he freed her.

practice: Think of something good you once had and lost track of: a friendship, a habit, a sense of wonder, a way of praying. Don't scold yourself for falling asleep on it; the viceroy slept seventy years and still got up.
Just ask where you might look for it now, one place, one small first step, and if you pray, ask for help finding it.

wordCard.voice: Viceroy, the king's second-in-command who set out to find a lost princess in Rebbe Nachman's first tale, failing, sleeping, waking, and searching until he found what was lost.

orig.note: Hebrew: the loss of a king's daughter, the name of Rebbe Nachman's first tale.

carryVoice: Your line: keep searching. Failing twice, even sleeping seventy years, doesn't end the story. See you tomorrow.
